sm: Albert Mohler opens with a Wall Street Journal article on parents taking a lenient approach to teen drinking. He says he is shocked that some parents give their teenagers fake IDs, drive them to parties where alcohol is served, and let them drink at home. The article links part of the shift to the pandemic, citing a study in which about one in six parents who once had zero tolerance later allowed underage drinking at home. Mohler points to the Bible's warnings about intoxication and notes that the practice is illegal and carries real liability.

He says the larger issue is parents who reject authority in favor of being friends with their children. He cites a psychologist who asks what it takes to get adults to act like adults, and notes that underage drinking is tied to sexual and abusive behavior. He then turns to a second Journal piece about parents suing schools over bad grades, including a case where a father sued a Palo Alto district over an AI-detection flag on his son's essay. Mohler says four in ten teachers report pressure to change grades, and that parents now even call their grown children's supervisors. He closes by saying that rejecting the right order set out in Scripture leaves disorder.

Mohler begins his listener questions with a letter from a member of Congress who was reelected but is weighing his calling after a midterm in which conservative voters did not turn out. Mohler says he is thankful for officials with such convictions and prays for him, urging him to lean on a faithful local church. He warns of what happens if such statesmen leave public life. Next, a 25-year-old pastor asks how to address progressive Christianity. Mohler advises being clear about what is at stake in doctrine and letting its proponents speak for themselves.

A young man asks about reading widely beyond the Puritans and modern evangelical works. Mohler says Christians are responsible for what they read. He keeps a wall of Puritans but also reads broadly to understand the world and how arguments are made, and he advises discussing reading within the church. A mother in Estonia then asks whether her four-year-old daughter, who wants to be baptized, may take communion. Mohler sides with her husband, saying baptism comes before the Lord's Supper and that parents can tell a child to wait. He says that when the gospel seizes a child's heart, the rest follows.
